passages.title: Sunday Trip
sentences: On Sunday, Sam went to the train museum with Grandma Rose.
They saw a big black steam train.
Sam climbed into the driver's seat.
Then they rode a small train around the park.
Sam bought a postcard of the steam train.
He put it on his wall at home.

passages.title: Leo's Spelling Test
sentences: Leo had a spelling test on Friday.
He studied the words every night.
On Friday, he spelled every word right.
After the test, Ben asked, "Was it hard?"
Leo grinned and said, "It was a piece of cake!"
Ben laughed and said, "You studied a lot!"

passages.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
sentences: All summer, a grasshopper played music and sang in a sunny field.
Nearby, an ant worked hard every day.
She carried seeds to her nest, one at a time.
"Come and sing with me!" said the grasshopper.
"I am saving food for the winter," said the ant, and she kept working.
Soon winter came, and snow covered the field.
The grasshopper looked for food, but the field was empty.
Cold and hungry, he walked to the ant's nest and asked for something to eat.
The ant had plenty of food, and she shared some seeds with him.
"Next summer, I will save food too," said the grasshopper.

credit.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Art Show
sentences: On Friday night, Maya's comic was in the school art show.
She had to talk about it in front of the parents.
Before her turn, Ben gave her a thumbs-up.
"Break a leg!" he said with a smile.
Maya laughed and walked to the front of the room.
She talked about her comic, and everyone clapped.
Ana stayed home that night.
She had a cold and felt under the weather.
After the show, Maya sent her a photo of the comic.

passages.title: The Fox and the Grapes
sentences: One hot afternoon, a hungry fox walked slowly along an old stone wall.
Above the wall, a bunch of ripe purple grapes hung from a twisting vine.
The grapes looked sweet and full of juice, and the fox wanted them very much.
He stepped back, ran forward and jumped as high as he possibly could.
His nose was still far below the lowest grapes.
He tried again and again, but every jump was too short.
At last, the fox sat down on the warm ground, tired and thirsty.
He looked up at the grapes one more time, and then he turned and walked away.
"Those grapes are probably sour anyway," he said. "I did not want them."

credit.title: The Fox and the Grapes
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Priya's Big Day
sentences: The Harbor Town robot contest was on Saturday at the library.
All week, Priya worked on her rover after school.
On Thursday, she also had a science quiz.
"I need to hit the books tonight," she told her mom.
She read her science notes at the kitchen table until bedtime.
On Saturday, Priya's rover drove through the maze in fifty seconds.
The judges gave her the blue ribbon for first place.
Sam, Maya and Leo cheered from the front row.
On the walk home, Priya held the ribbon and smiled the whole way.
"I'm on cloud nine," she said to Sam.
Sam laughed and said, "I can tell!"

passages.title: The Lion and the Mouse
sentences: A big lion was sleeping in the warm sun.
A small mouse ran across his paw and woke him up.
The lion grabbed the mouse with his huge paw.
"Please let me go," said the mouse. "One day I will help you."
The lion smiled at the idea of such a tiny helper, but he let the mouse go.
A few days later, the lion stepped into a rope net in the tall grass.
He pulled and pulled, but the ropes held him tight.
The mouse heard the lion roar and ran to him.
She chewed through the ropes with her sharp teeth.
Soon the lion was free.
The lion thanked the mouse, and they became good friends.

credit.title: The Lion and the Mouse
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Shepherd Boy and the Wolf
sentences: A shepherd boy had a job watching the sheep on a hill near a village.
The days were long and quiet, and he felt bored.
One morning, he shouted, "Wolf! A wolf is chasing the sheep!"
The people in the village ran up the hill to help.
They saw only sheep eating grass, and the boy laughed.
The next day, he played the same trick again.
Then one evening, a real wolf came out of the woods.
The boy shouted "Wolf!" as loudly as he could.
This time, the people thought it was another trick, so they stayed home.
The wolf chased the sheep far away into the hills.

credit.title: The Shepherd Boy and the Wolf
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The North Wind and the Sun
sentences: One day, the North Wind and the Sun argued about which of them was stronger.
Just then, they saw a traveler walking down a road in a warm coat.
"Let us see who can make him take off his coat," said the Sun.
The North Wind went first.
He blew a cold, hard wind at the traveler.
But the harder he blew, the tighter the traveler held his coat around him.
At last, the North Wind stopped trying.
Then the Sun came out from behind a cloud.
She shone gently and warmly on the traveler.
Soon the traveler felt hot, so he opened his coat.
Then he took it off and sat down in the shade of a tree.

credit.title: The North Wind and the Sun
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

items.prompt: Priya said, "I need to hit the books tonight." What did she mean?
options: She needs to study hard.
She wants to hit her books with her hand.
She needs to buy new books.
items.hint: Look at what Priya has to get ready for. Then look at what she does that night.
items.explain: "Hit the books" means study hard. Priya had a quiz, and she read her notes until bedtime. The words are not meant literally.

Grandma Rose's bakery
how to buy a postcard

items.explain: "On Sunday, Sam went to the train museum with Grandma Rose" tells what the whole story is about. It is the first sentence.

items.prompt: Leo said, "It was a piece of cake!" What did he mean?
options: The test was easy.
He ate cake at the test.
The test was about food.
items.hint: Look at how Leo did on the test. Then think about what he wants Ben to know.
items.explain: "A piece of cake" means very easy. Leo means the test was easy for him. The words are not meant literally, because there was no cake.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences. Does each one mean exactly what it says, or something else?

cards.text: Grandma Rose gave Leo a piece of cake.
The spelling test was a piece of cake.
Leo studied the words every night.
That math sheet was a piece of cake!

items.hint: Ask: is there real cake here? If it is about a test or a sheet, the words mean something else.
items.explain: A test or a math sheet that is "a piece of cake" is easy, so those mean something else. Grandma Rose giving Leo cake is real cake, so it means exactly what it says.

items.prompt: What is this story mostly about?
options: Ben's birthday cake
Leo's easy spelling test
Leo's new skateboard
items.hint: Think about what all the sentences talk about. Remember what "a piece of cake" means.
items.explain: The story is mostly about Leo's spelling test. He studied, spelled every word right, and said it was easy.

items.prompt: Fill in the story map for this fable.

slots.label: What happens
options: A grasshopper teaches an ant to sing.
An ant saves food, and a grasshopper learns to get ready for winter.
An ant and a grasshopper build a nest.

slots.label: The lesson
options: Singing is better than working.
Snow is good for fields.
Get ready now for what you will need later.

items.hint: For the first box, think about the whole story. For the lesson, look at what the grasshopper says at the end.
items.explain: The ant saves food, and the grasshopper learns to get ready for winter. The lesson is to get ready now for what you will need later.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence where the ant says why she is working.
items.hint: Find the words the ant says. Look for the season she is thinking about.
items.explain: "I am saving food for the winter," said the ant. That is why she works all summer.

items.prompt: Ben said, "Break a leg!" What did he mean?
options: Stand on one leg.
Good luck!
Walk slowly.
items.hint: Look at when Ben said it and what his hand and face did.
items.explain: "Break a leg" means good luck. People say it to someone before a show. Ben is wishing Maya well, so the words are not meant literally.

items.prompt: Ana felt "under the weather." What does that mean?
options: She stood out in the rain.
She felt a little sick.
She felt excited.
items.hint: Read the same sentence again. Look at what Ana had.
items.explain: "Under the weather" means a little sick. Ana had a cold. The words are not meant literally, because she was at home, not out in the weather.

items.prompt: What is this story mostly about?
options: Ana's cold
Maya's comic at the art show
Ben's soccer game
items.hint: Think about what most of the sentences talk about, not just one.
items.explain: The story is mostly about Maya's comic at the art show. Most sentences tell about her turn at the show.

items.prompt: What is the lesson of this story?
options: Foxes are good at jumping.
Sometimes people say a thing is bad because they failed to get it.
Grapes taste sour on hot days.
items.hint: A lesson is an idea for your own life. Compare what the fox wanted at the start with what he said at the end.
items.explain: The lesson is that people sometimes say a thing is bad because they failed to get it. The fox wanted the grapes, then called them sour after he failed to reach them.

items.prompt: Why did the fox say the grapes were sour?
options: He tasted one, and it was sour.
Another fox told him.
He was upset that he failed to reach them.
items.hint: Check if the fox ever tasted a grape. Then look at what happened just before he spoke.
items.explain: The fox was upset that he failed to reach the grapes. He never tasted one, so calling them sour made him feel better.

items.prompt: What is this story mostly about?
options: A fox tries hard to reach some grapes, then walks away.
A fox builds a stone wall.
A fox shares grapes with a friend.
items.hint: Think about what the fox does in most of the sentences.
items.explain: The story is mostly about a fox who tries hard to reach some grapes and then walks away. Most sentences tell about his jumps.

items.prompt: Priya said, "I'm on cloud nine." What did she mean?
options: She is up in the sky.
She is very happy.
She is very tired.
She can see nine clouds.
items.hint: Look at what just happened to Priya and what her face is doing.
items.explain: "On cloud nine" means very, very happy. Priya won first place and smiled the whole way home. The words are not meant literally.

items.prompt: What is this story mostly about?
options: Priya's science quiz
Sam's walk home
Priya's hard work and her win at the robot contest
items.hint: Think about what the story talks about from start to end, not just one part.
items.explain: The story is mostly about Priya's hard work and her win at the robot contest. It starts with the contest and ends with her blue ribbon.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences. Does each one mean exactly what it says, or something else?

cards.text: Priya read her notes until bedtime.
I need to hit the books tonight.
The judges gave her the blue ribbon.
Sam, Maya and Leo cheered from the front row.

items.hint: Picture each sentence. If the picture would be strange, the words mean something else.
items.explain: "On cloud nine", "hit the books", "break a leg" and "under the weather" mean something else: happy, study, good luck and a little sick. The other sentences mean exactly what they say.

items.prompt: What is the lesson of this story?
options: Lions sleep in the sun all day.
Small friends can be a big help.
Mice like to chew rope.
items.hint: A lesson is an idea for your own life. Think about who helped whom at the end.
items.explain: The lesson is that small friends can be a big help. The tiny mouse freed the big lion from the net.

items.prompt: What is the lesson of this story?
options: Wolves only come out in the evening.
Tell the truth, so people will believe you when you need help.
Watching sheep is a quiet job.
items.hint: A lesson is an idea for your own life. Think about why the people stayed home the last time.
items.explain: The lesson is to tell the truth, so people will believe you when you need help. The boy tricked the people twice, so they stayed home when the real wolf came.

items.prompt: What is the lesson of this story?
options: The wind is stronger than the sun.
Always wear a coat on a trip.
Being gentle can work better than being rough.
items.hint: A lesson is an idea for your own life. Compare what the Wind did with what the Sun did.
items.explain: The lesson is that being gentle can work better than being rough. The hard wind made the traveler hold his coat tight, but the Sun's gentle warmth made him take it off.
